title: The Four Kingdoms
lead: Daniel 2 (a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron and iron-and-clay) and Daniel 7 (four beasts) describe a sequence of four kingdoms ended by the kingdom of God. Only the first, Babylon, is named in chapter 2; chapters 8 and 11 name Persia and Greece. Jews and Christians have identified the four in two main ways, with Rome as the fourth in the older tradition and Greece in most critical scholarship, and the choice decides when the stone is thought to strike.

sections.b: Nebuchadnezzar's statue has a head of gold, chest and arms of silver, belly and thighs of bronze, legs of iron and feet of iron mixed with clay (Daniel 2:31-33). Daniel says the head is Nebuchadnezzar (2:38), a second kingdom is lower, a third of bronze rules the whole earth, a fourth is strong as iron and breaks the rest, and its feet are a divided kingdom, partly strong and partly brittle (2:39-43). A stone cut "not by hands" strikes the feet, the statue is ground to chaff, and the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth: a kingdom God will set up that will never be ruined (2:34-35, 44-45).

The critical majority (John Collins, Louis Hartman and Alexander Di Lella, and others) counts four separate kingdoms: Babylon, then Media, then Persia, then Alexander's empire and its successors. A Median kingdom between Babylon and Persia rests on prophecies such as Isaiah 13:17 and Jeremiah 51:11, 28 and on the book's own Darius the Mede (5:31; 6:1). The iron kingdom is Greek power; the feet of iron and clay are the Seleucid and Ptolemaic kingdoms, joined by marriages that did not hold (Daniel 11:6, 17); the stone is God's own act that ends the Greek kings. It fits the book's late setting and the detail of chapter 11.
sections.refs: Daniel 2:39-43; Daniel 7:3-7; Daniel 8:20-21; Daniel 11:2-4; Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11

sections.b: Most Christian interpreters from the early church on (Hippolytus, Jerome, and the Reformers including Calvin) take Media and Persia as one kingdom (compare 8:20, "the kings of Media and Persia") and the fourth as Rome. The rabbis too often name the fourth "Edom", their word for Rome (for example Genesis Rabbah 2:4; Leviticus Rabbah 13:5). The feet are the divided later Roman world; the stone is Christ and his kingdom, begun at his coming (Irenaeus, Hippolytus, Jerome, Calvin), or the Messiah in the Jewish reading. Josephus declined to explain the stone (Antiquities 10.210).

sections.h: View 3: the fourth kingdom in a last form
sections.b: Futurist readers (for example John Walvoord) keep Rome as the fourth and look for a final form of it, a revived empire of ten kings, which the stone strikes at the second coming; the kingdom that fills the earth is then Christ's future reign. Others who hold Rome as the fourth hold that the stone has already struck and the kingdom is growing, as in the older Christian reading.

A scheme of four ages in metals appears in Hesiod (Works and Days 109-201, with a fifth, heroic age); Greek and Roman writers listed four empires, Assyria, Media, Persia, Macedonia (Aemilius Sura in Velleius Paterculus 1.6.6), and the Sibylline Oracles (book 4) do the same. Scholars debate whether Daniel borrowed the pattern or shares an older common one (David Flusser; John Collins).

sections.h: Daniel 11 and the last two kingdoms
sections.b: Daniel 11 returns to the kingdoms of chapters 2 and 7 but names only Persia and Greece. It lists four Persian kings (the fourth, far richer than the rest, is usually taken as Xerxes) and then a mighty king whose kingdom is broken and divided to the four winds, as Alexander's realm was divided (11:2–4). In the critical schema, where the four kingdoms are Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece, this is the end of the sequence. Readers who count Rome as the fourth kingdom point to the "ships of Kittim" in 11:30, a name for the western sea powers that some take as Rome.
